headline: A rare dinosaur skeleton sells for 47.3 million dollars

sources.title: Nanotyrannus: Dinosaur skeleton sells for $47.3m in New York auction (BBC News)
Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m at New York auction (The Guardian)
Rare Nanotyrannus 'Jodi' sells at auction for $47.3 million (CNN)

chunks.text: On October 27, 2026, a rare dinosaur skeleton sold for 47.3 million dollars at an [[auction]] in New York. At an auction, buyers keep raising their offers. The [[auction house]] expected 6 to 9 million dollars. Six [[bidders]] competed for 12 minutes, and the [[final price]] {{shot up}} to more than five times the top [[estimate]]. The buyer has not {{come forward}}. Only one dinosaur, a T. rex, has sold for more.

verbs.why: Gas prices shoot up every summer. Rents shoot up when a big new company comes to town. The final price shot up to more than five times the top estimate.

verbs.correct: To let the public know who you are
verbs.wrong: To pay the full price at once
verbs.why: Some big donors never come forward. Some lottery winners never come forward. The buyer has not come forward.

chunks.text: For decades, many experts {{mixed up}} this kind of dinosaur with a young T. rex. In 2023, this skeleton was shown at an [[art fair]] in London as a young T. rex. Then, in October 2025, a study by U.S. researchers found it was a [[separate]] kind of dinosaur. It {{turned out}} to be a smaller, [[slimmer]] [[cousin]] of T. rex. The auction house says its bones show it was an adult, not a teenager.

verbs.correct: To think one thing is another thing
verbs.wrong: To invent a story about something
verbs.why: Many people mix up these two words. I often mix up the twins in my class. For decades, many experts mixed up this kind of dinosaur with another, more famous one.

verbs.correct: To be shown to be something in the end
verbs.wrong: To be worth a great deal of money
verbs.why: A cheap old painting sometimes turns out to be very valuable. A strange noise at night usually turns out to be the wind. This skeleton turned out to belong to a separate, slimmer kind of dinosaur.

chunks.text: In 2019, a [[rancher]] found the skeleton on her land in Montana, a western U.S. state. It is named after her. Its bones are [[fossils]], ancient [[remains]] that slowly changed into rock. A [[fossil hunter]] later {{dug it up}}. It has about 191 bones and a nearly complete [[skull]]. It is one of only three good skeletons of its kind. It is the first to {{come up}} for sale since the 2025 study.

verbs.correct: To remove something from the ground
verbs.wrong: To clean old bones with a brush
verbs.why: Farmers sometimes dig up old coins in their fields. City workers dig up the street to fix the pipes. A professional fossil hunter dug up the skeleton after a rancher found it.
Houses on this street rarely come up for sale. Good jobs at the hospital come up only a few times a year. This skeleton is the first of its kind to come up for sale since the 2025 study.

chunks.text: Some [[paleontologists]], scientists who study fossils, worry about the sale. A professor at a university in Scotland {{spoke out}} against it. He said scientists had just {{found out}} this dinosaur was real. Now a [[private collector]] could keep it {{locked away}}, he said. A paleontologist at the University of Maryland said some U.S. museums are {{closing down}} or may close because of [[money problems]]. But a British paleontologist said many fossils like this {{end up}} in museums in time.

verbs.correct: To say what you think in public
verbs.wrong: To raise money for a museum
verbs.why: Many parents speak out when schools lose money. She always speaks out when she sees something unfair. A professor in Scotland spoke out against the sale of the skeleton.
Students find out their grades online. We usually find out the winner at the end of the show. He said scientists had only just found out this dinosaur was real.

verbs.correct: To keep something hidden and safe
verbs.wrong: To sell something to a museum
verbs.why: My grandmother locks away her jewelry when guests visit. Museums lock away their most fragile objects in storage. He said a private collector could keep the skeleton locked away.

verbs.correct: To shut for the last time
verbs.wrong: To open fewer days each week
verbs.why: Small shops close down when rents get too high. Many factories close down when orders stop. A paleontologist said some American museums are closing down or may close because of money problems.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a place
verbs.wrong: To be shown for a short time
verbs.why: Lost socks often end up under the bed. Old phones often end up in a drawer. A British paleontologist said many fossils like this end up in museums in time.

mainIdea.s: A dinosaur that experts once mixed up with a young T. rex sold for 47.3 million dollars in New York. Some scientists worry a private buyer could keep the skeleton from the public.
mainIdea.why: The skeleton turned out to be its own kind of dinosaur. A paleontologist spoke out because it could be locked away by a private collector.

mainIdea.s: A natural history museum paid a huge sum for a rare T. rex cousin at an auction. Scientists are happy because they can now study the bones and show the full skeleton to visitors.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the buyer did not come forward, and nobody knows who it is. Some scientists worry the skeleton could be locked away from the public.

mainIdea.s: Researchers in Montana say they have discovered a new kind of dinosaur under a large farm. They believe its bones prove that young T. rex grew much faster than anyone had thought.
mainIdea.why: This is about a rare skeleton that sold at auction in New York. The price shot up to far more than experts expected.

lines.text: Did you see the news about the dinosaur skeleton that sold in New York?
I did. 47.3 million dollars is a [[jaw-dropping]] price.
The auction house expected 6 to 9 million. The final price {{shot up}} way higher than that.
Nobody knows. The buyer didn't {{come forward}}.
That's the fun part. For years, experts {{mixed up}} this kind of dinosaur with a young T. rex.
It {{turned out}} to be a smaller, slimmer cousin. Only three good skeletons are known.
That explains the price. When something that rare {{comes up}} for sale, [[the sky's the limit]].
Right. A rancher found it on her land in Montana, and a fossil hunter {{dug it up}}.
Are scientists happy about the sale?
Not really. One paleontologist {{spoke out}}. He worries it could be {{locked away}} in a private collection.
Prices like that are [[out of reach]] for most museums.
Another expert said some U.S. museums are {{closing down}} or could close because of money problems.
Millions for one skeleton while museums close? That [[makes my head spin]].
But a British paleontologist said many fossils like this {{end up}} in museums in time.
I hope so. I'd love to see it with my own eyes.

ex: The view from the top of the mountain is jaw-dropping.

expressions.def: Used to say there is no limit to how high or far something can go

expressions.def: Too expensive or too difficult for someone to get
ex: A house in this city is out of reach for most young families.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is so big, fast or strange that it confuses you
ex: All these new phone plans make my head spin.
